analysis.title: US midterm elections: What a Democratic sweep means for the economic outlook
key_insights: Democrats won both chambers in the midterms. The NYT nowcast has them at 250+ House seats, the largest House majority since 2008. They are on course to gain eight Senate seats for a 55-45 majority, the strongest since 2012.
Large majorities give Democrats room to set the agenda and write legislation. The Senate filibuster and presidential veto still constrain enacting major policy changes.
Democrats are expected to push healthcare, other social spending and clean energy through reconciliation bills, which need only a simple majority.

Government funding expires December 11, during the lame-duck session with Republicans still in control. Limited agreement on full-year appropriations makes a short-term continuing resolution the most likely outcome, pushing the next deadline into early 2027 and keeping shutdown risk alive.
The debt ceiling could be reached around Q2 2027 under current spending plans. Extraordinary measures could push the 'X date' toward year-end.

Fidelity sees risks tilted toward greater fiscal easing. It sees limited inclination from either party to rein in the elevated deficit despite strong growth and the One Big Beautiful Bill fiscal boost this year.

A Democratic House opens the door to investigations into the administration's business dealings and prediction markets, and possible impeachment proceedings. Removal would need a two-thirds Senate majority, so the main effect is headline risk and lost political bandwidth.
A Democratic Senate could block key appointments, including to the Fed.

Democrats flipped four governorships, including Texas, Ohio and Georgia, which hold almost a third of planned US data centre capacity. Governors who campaigned on curbing data centres are likely to add moratoria and permit restrictions, which could slow AI infrastructure investment.
The data centre risk is mostly state-level for now, but could become federal ahead of the 2028 elections. Fidelity calls it a key risk to its macro outlook.

Trump keeps wide discretion over tariffs, immigration and foreign policy. Section 301 investigations into industrial overcapacity are being prepared to replace tariffs struck down under IEEPA, so trade restrictions stay a central tool.
Fidelity sees upside risks to oil prices from the Iran war. Energy-importing Europe and Asia face inflation pressure and a bias toward monetary tightening.

Little scope for easing in US-China tensions. Tariffs, technology restrictions and supply-chain diversification have bipartisan support. Semiconductor export controls are in the executive's remit, which matters for Taiwan, South Korea and China.
Base case is US growth slowing to trend next year after robust 2026 growth, alongside a renewed Fed hiking cycle, tightening financial conditions and building geopolitical and inflationary shocks.

sector_views.rationale: State-level data centre moratoria and permit restrictions in Democratic-flipped states could slow AI capex. The AI build-out is also shifting from the scale of spending to the returns it generates.

tension_points.bull_case: Democratic leverage at funding and debt ceiling deadlines, plus bipartisan reluctance to cut the deficit, tilts risks toward more fiscal easing and supports growth.
tension_points.bear_case: The filibuster and veto limit what Democrats can enact, and a short-term continuing resolution keeps shutdown risk alive.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A full-year appropriations deal that cuts spending before the December 11 deadline, or a shutdown that extends into early 2027.

tension_points.bull_case: Federal policy is largely unchanged and the restrictions are mostly state-level, so the AI build-out continues.
tension_points.bear_case: Democratic governors in Texas, Ohio and Georgia impose moratoria and permit limits, and the issue could go federal ahead of 2028.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Moratoria or new permit restrictions in Texas, Ohio or Georgia, or federal action on data centre regulation.
